source_notes: The pinned source is the 26-page final published PDF. Page 23 describes an external supplement; it is not the beginning of an appendix body inside this PDF. References end on page 26. The supplement was not opened.

All six actual main-text Theorems are preserved. Lemmas, Corollaries, Remarks and citations are not additional theorem records. Corollary 4.5 contributes hypotheses because Theorem 4.6 explicitly invokes them.

Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 4.6 both contain substantial material after their initial conclusions. All of that italic material is included; in particular Theorem 4.6 includes the total-risk and expected-distance bounds.
The unnumbered Assumption prints the conditioning index y in Omega although the conditional kernel domain uses Omega_Y. This source notation is retained.

The central class consists of all square-integrable central-field-measurable functions and can be infinite dimensional. It is not the span of the d generating coordinates and is not inherently mean-zero.

Remark 3.3 declares all functions mean-zero. The later class of neural networks with biases is not explicitly centered. Since centered losses and variance penalties are translation invariant, proportionality up to sign in Theorem 3.7 and distance to plus/minus a function require attention to that convention; no centering operation is inserted into the source estimator.

GMDD uses a Levy measure and a cndf-induced difference kernel. Full integrability, symmetry and support conditions sufficient for the displayed equivalence and zero-characterization are not provided here. The main text points to external references [4,35]. No unverified extra conditions are presented as original assumptions.
The Levy measure mu in Section 2.2 and the later scalar/vector optimization penalties reuse the same letter with different meanings. Tilde-mu is a separate cross-direction penalty.

Theorem 3.2 assumes an optimizer exists. Its upper bound m<=dimension of the full central class does not independently ensure enough nonconstant normalized directions. The theorem is not rewritten as an existence assertion.
Assumption A1 requires distinct first d+1 ordered negative GMDD values, not just the first d. It also constrains tilde-mu. Theorem 3.8 does not state A1.
The Frobenius penalty is unsquared; the successive variance and covariance penalties are squared. Theorem 3.8 is a population claim and does not refer to the separate empirical implementation.

The sample passage defines D_n from observed pairs but does not explicitly write an iid assumption there. The U-statistic analysis uses independent observations in its prose; the exact general sampling assumption and measurable argmin selections need specification in formalization.

The order-four empirical objectives require a meaningful inverse binomial(n,4), ordinarily n>=4. Theorem 4.2 states n>=V and has an n-3 denominator, while Theorem 4.4 does not explicitly restate either restriction. No extra restriction is inserted into the original bodies.

I_{n,k} contains all ordered distinct-index tuples; J_{n,k} contains only increasing tuples. The kernels use I_{4,k}, while the U-statistic average uses J_{n,4}. All printed coefficients are retained.

The empirical recursion uses previous estimated directions; the excess risk fixes previous population directions. The first-direction estimator uses no covariance kernel, so Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 do not inherit the later-step kernel merely because it occurs nearby.

A2 bounds all candidate functions and the kernel at every pair of response-space points. Its prose says bounded Y can ensure boundedness, but that does not literally bound a kernel on all R^q. A2 also requires a uniform bound on a candidate class otherwise described by architecture alone.

The Holder definition is restricted to beta in (0,1] and a function-dependent existential zeta on the unit cube. No common Holder radius, derivative-based extension or explicit support reduction of the general X law is supplied in that definition.

A4 does not specify the range of epsilon. Its right-hand side becomes negative for sufficiently large epsilon, so an unrestricted all-positive-epsilon reading is not silently imposed. V depends on the candidate class and may therefore depend on n.

The sign-invariant rho is a pseudodistance on the unquotiented function space. C1 is only specified as an appropriate positive constant satisfying (12); its detailed choice is delegated to the excluded proof of Theorem 4.4.

Theorem 4.6 retains probability 1-(4j-3)delta for each j and then a summed bound. It does not separately state the simultaneous event probability for that sum; do not silently add a union bound or uniformity in d.

The last Theorem 4.6 clause invokes a ReLU class with a stated sample-dependent depth that is not rounded to an integer. The width parameter N is arbitrary, and the sample-size condition uses the resulting S and L. The generic positive-constant convention asserts independence of n, not independence of every architecture parameter.

Section 4.2 contains proof-level notational inconsistencies: R1,n is written with an extra argument in one L1,n term and the displayed first-order sum omits the 1/n that appears in v1,n. These formulas are not theorem targets and are not substituted into the empirical estimator or rho definition.

Selection of tuning constants and the empirical Frobenius estimator are delegated to the supplement; the dimension-selection algorithm, simulation optimizer Adam and numerical examples are downstream uses, not hypotheses of these six Theorems.

ambient_resolution.shared: A1 fixes X in R^p, Y in R^q and the underlying probability/conditional distributions. D1 fixes the nonlinear SDR map and known intrinsic dimension d. D2 is the unnumbered domination and normalization Assumption; D3 is the entire central class. D4 fixes the response difference kernel, with Levy-measure conditions not fully specified in the main text. The tilde pair in D5 is a joint independent copy. A2 and A3 resolve function norms and product L2 spaces; I_d is the identity matrix. Expectations, covariance, conditional independence, orthogonality, positive semidefinite matrices, extrema, finite sums and standard real arithmetic are ambient. A4 defines both tuple conventions used in U-statistics. A5 fixes sample-size independence of generic constants. A6 is the original zero-mean convention inside Remark 3.3; its scope and compatibility with later uncentered candidate networks are not silently strengthened. The source uses script D_n for observed pairs without a separate explicit iid statement at that definition; probabilistic sampling and measurable argmin conventions remain to be clarified for formalization. Theorem statements are transcriptions, not certifications of the claimed results.
ambient_resolution.3.2: The theorem binds m, vector f-star, its components, the GMDD matrix and ordered negative values lambda-star, and centered components bar-f-star. D3 supplies the central class, D4 the response kernel and D5 the GMDD meaning. The entire selection and ordering convention is inside the theorem. No A1 strict gap, network class, empirical estimator or exhaustive recovery condition is added. The assertion is conditional on an optimal solution existing; dimension of the central class is not by itself an existence proof for all normalized optimizers.
ambient_resolution.3.7: D9 is the explicit (A1) restriction on the first d+1 ordered values and tilde-mu; D6 gives those values and the selected original directions. D7 resolves the alternative equation (7) reference. D8 supplies the penalized minimizer f-star_{j,mu_j}, positive mu_j, tilde-mu and preceding penalized directions. The two signs and scale sqrt(1-lambda-star_j/(2mu_j)) are retained. This population identification theorem has no empirical candidate class or sample-size restriction.
ambient_resolution.3.8: D10 is the unsquared Frobenius-penalty loss. Its minimizing vector and scalar mu are bound in the statement, D3 supplies the central class and D6 supplies ordered values plus objective (6). The first conclusion assumes only the stated positive mu; the equivalence conclusion adds mu greater than the absolute sum. Theorem 3.7 and A1 are not imported as extra hypotheses. The empirical LF estimator is outside these statements and is delegated to the supplement.
ambient_resolution.4.2: The first-direction slow-rate statement in Section 4.1 uses A7 (d=1). D9, D16 and D20 resolve the explicit A1, A2 and A4 hypotheses. D8 resolves L1 and the population minimizer; D14 is the first global empirical minimizer, using D12 but not the later covariance kernel D13. D11 is the function class in the approximation infimum, D19 defines its covering numbers through A4, and A2 supplies the uniform norm. Preserve n>=V and n-3 exactly. No Holder class, ReLU architecture or A3 is inserted.
ambient_resolution.4.4: The first-direction fast-rate statement retains A1, A2 and A4 through D9, D16 and D20. D8 and D14 distinguish the population optimum and first empirical minimizer. D22 is rho up to sign, whose constant is tied to (12) via the first-order loss in D21 and kernel D12. The displayed approximation infimum is over D11. The statement has no explicit n>=V restriction, A3 or specialized network architecture. A proof decomposition, Rademacher average and its minimizer do not replace the estimator in the theorem.
ambient_resolution.4.6: The first clause inherits A1, A2 and A4 from Theorem 4.4. D25 supplies the sequential empirical direction, with previous estimated directions in its objective; D8 supplies previous population directions in the risk. D15 supplies R_j and total R, and D22 supplies rho. A(n,V,delta) is completely bound inside the statement and does not require another API. The per-j probability is 1-(4j-3)delta; a simultaneous event for all j is not separately stated. The summed-risk consequence and final expectation are still in the italic theorem body. Only the last clause invokes D24, the hypotheses of Corollary 4.5, including D23 architecture, D17 (A3), D18 Holder class and the stated sample-size condition. Corollary 4.5 is not added as another theorem. Its beta in (0,1] comes from Section 2.1, and its depth expression has no printed integer rounding.
